title: The Alignment Problem
subtitle: Machine Learning and Human Values
pitch: A beautifully told history of how machine learning systems learn the wrong lessons, from biased predictions to reward hacking, and the researchers trying to fix it.

chapters.g: A short opening scene from the early history of neural networks.
Introduces the alignment problem: the gap between what we want and what we actually train systems to do.
How systems learn from data, and how biased data, like word embeddings that absorb stereotypes, leads to biased systems.
The fight over risk assessment tools in criminal justice, and the discovery that different fairness definitions cannot all be met at once.
Why it matters that we can see inside models, and early work on explaining what neural networks have learned.
The history of reinforcement learning, from animal psychology to modern agents that learn from rewards.
How the way we hand out rewards shapes behaviour, and how agents exploit badly designed rewards.
Giving agents an inner drive to explore, and the surprising ways curiosity can go wrong.
Learning by copying humans, and its limits when the student needs to do better than the teacher.
Inverse reinforcement learning and learning from human feedback: working out what people want from what they do.
Why systems that know what they do not know are safer, including the off switch problem and corrigibility.
Pulls the threads together: alignment is both a technical and a human problem, and it is already here.

ideas: Today's fairness failures and tomorrow's catastrophic risks are the same kind of problem.
Systems learn what you reward, not what you mean.
Learning from human feedback is powerful but imperfect.
Uncertainty and humility make systems safer.

args.a: Near term harms and long term risks belong to one alignment problem.
args.c: Some fairness researchers see long term risk talk as a distraction, and some x-risk researchers think fairness work does not scale to superintelligence.

args.a: Learning from human behaviour can tell machines our values.
args.c: Human behaviour is inconsistent and sometimes bad, so copying it can copy our flaws.

questions: Which story in the book surprised you most?
Is it possible to make one fairness definition work for everyone?
Where in your own life do incentives create 'reward hacking'?

quiz.q: What are the three parts of the book?
quiz.w: The parts move from prediction to action to values.

quiz.q: What did researchers find about fairness definitions?
o: Some cannot all be satisfied at once
quiz.w: Different reasonable fairness criteria can conflict mathematically.
It works backwards from behaviour to the reward that explains it.
